bob-dylan.about: His debut, produced by John Hammond, the Columbia talent scout who had signed him. It is mostly folk and blues standards, with just two of his own songs: Talkin' New York and Song to Woody, a tribute to Woody Guthrie. It sold slowly at first and only charted in the UK in 1965, once he was famous.
bob-dylan.cover: A young, round-faced Dylan in a sheepskin-collared jacket, photographed by Don Hunstein.
influence: Song to Woody marked the start of a lifelong habit of writing about the people and records that shaped him.

freewheelin-bob-dylan.about: The record where he became a songwriter first and a folk singer second: eleven of its thirteen songs are his own. It opens with Blowin' in the Wind, a hit for Peter, Paul and Mary within weeks, and also holds Masters of War, A Hard Rain's a-Gonna Fall and Don't Think Twice, It's All Right. After it, at 22, he was treated as a major artist.
freewheelin-bob-dylan.cover: Dylan and his girlfriend Suze Rotolo walking arm in arm down the middle of Jones Street in Greenwich Village in February 1963, photographed by Don Hunstein a short walk from their apartment.
influence: Cameron Crowe recreated the cover for Vanilla Sky (2001), with Tom Cruise and Penélope Cruz walking down a snowy New York street.
Todd Haynes restaged it in his Dylan film I'm Not There (2007).
It was a visual reference for the Coen brothers' Inside Llewyn Davis (2013) and for A Complete Unknown (2024).
A copy of the LP is a prop in a key scene of Jacques Rivette's film L'Amour fou (1969).
Blowin' in the Wind became one of the anthems of the 1960s civil rights movement.

the-times-they-are-a-changin.about: His first album of entirely original songs: stark, sparse ballads about racism, poverty and social change, recorded in the second half of 1963. The title song became one of the defining statements of the decade.
the-times-they-are-a-changin.cover: A black-and-white portrait of Dylan in a work shirt, photographed by Barry Feinstein.
influence: The title song opens the film Watchmen (2009) over its opening montage.
It was among the Dylan records that meant most to Steve Jobs, according to Walter Isaacson's biography, and turns up in the 2015 film Steve Jobs.
The song has been used in advertising, including for Coopers & Lybrand (sung by Richie Havens, 1994) and the Bank of Montreal (Pete Seeger, 1996).

another-side-of-bob-dylan.about: Recorded in a single night in June 1964, solo as before, but turning away from protest songs towards personal and surreal ones. Parts of the folk establishment complained he had lost touch; critics now see it as a bridge to what came next. It holds It Ain't Me, Babe, My Back Pages and Chimes of Freedom.
another-side-of-bob-dylan.cover: A black-and-white photograph of Dylan by Sandy Speiser.
influence: The Byrds had hits with versions of All I Really Want to Do (1965) and My Back Pages (1967).
It Ain't Me, Babe was a hit for the Turtles and a duet staple for Johnny Cash and June Carter.

bringing-it-all-back-home.about: His first album with an electric band, and his first US top-ten album. Side one is electric rock and roll; side two is mostly acoustic, including Mr. Tambourine Man and It's Alright, Ma (I'm Only Bleeding). The switch split the folk scene, and the protest songs gave way to surreal, complex writing.
bringing-it-all-back-home.cover: Daniel Kramer photographed Dylan with a softened-edge lens, with Sally Grossman, wife of his manager Albert Grossman, in the background. The room is scattered with LPs by the Impressions, Robert Johnson, Ravi Shankar, Lotte Lenya and Eric Von Schmidt, among other objects.
influence: The film clip for Subterranean Homesick Blues, with Dylan flipping cue cards, opened D. A. Pennebaker's Dont Look Back (1967) and is often called an early music video.
The Byrds' version of Mr. Tambourine Man went to number one in 1965 and helped start folk rock.
It is widely ranked among the greatest rock albums, including number 31 on Rolling Stone's 2003 list.

highway-61-revisited.about: A full rock band on every track except the eleven-minute closer, Desolation Row. It opens with Like a Rolling Stone, released as a single ahead of the album, and includes songs he still plays, from the title track to Ballad of a Thin Man. Author Michael Gray argued that in a real sense the 1960s started here.
highway-61-revisited.cover: Dylan on the front step of Albert Grossman's apartment in Gramercy Park, New York, photographed by Daniel Kramer, in a Triumph motorcycle T-shirt under a silk shirt. His friend Bob Neuwirth stands behind him, cut off at the waist, holding a camera.
influence: Like a Rolling Stone topped Rolling Stone's list of the greatest songs of all time in 2004 and 2010.
The poet Philip Larkin, reviewing it for the Daily Telegraph in 1965, found himself well rewarded by it.

blonde-on-blonde.about: A double album, mostly recorded in Nashville in February and March 1966 after slow sessions in New York, with Al Kooper, Robbie Robertson and top Nashville session players. Dylan later said it came closest to the sound he heard in his head, which he called that thin, wild mercury sound. It completed his run of three electric albums in fifteen months.
blonde-on-blonde.cover: A slightly blurred close-up of Dylan in a suede jacket and checked scarf, photographed by Jerry Schatzberg in New York. The gatefold opens into a three-quarter-length portrait, and the artist's name and title appear only on the spine.
influence: One of the first double albums by a major rock artist.
Rainy Day Women #12 & 35 reached number 2 in the US and I Want You made the top 20.

bob-dylans-greatest-hits.about: His first compilation, released in March 1967 while he was out of sight after his motorcycle accident. It gathers every top-40 single he had had, plus album tracks that other artists had turned into hits. Certified five times platinum, it is his best-selling album in the US.
bob-dylans-greatest-hits.cover: A backlit profile of Dylan on stage, photographed by Rowland Scherman at a concert in Washington, D.C. in November 1965. The design won the Grammy for best album cover photography.
influence: The original LP came with Milton Glaser's psychedelic poster of Dylan, with rainbow-coloured hair, one of the best-known posters of the 1960s.

john-wesley-harding.about: Short, spare songs recorded in Nashville with a tiny band, released with no publicity at the height of psychedelia. It came out of the same period as the Basement Tapes and topped the UK chart. It includes All Along the Watchtower and I'll Be Your Baby Tonight.
john-wesley-harding.cover: A squinting Dylan outdoors in Woodstock, flanked by two Bengali Baul musicians, Luxman and Purna Das, with local carpenter Charlie Joy behind him. The title borrows (and misspells) the name of the Texas outlaw John Wesley Hardin.
influence: Jimi Hendrix's 1968 version of All Along the Watchtower became the template Dylan himself later followed on stage.
Rumours spread that the faces of the Beatles were hidden in the tree on the cover.
Its plain, back-to-basics sound, released amid psychedelia, is often seen as an early sign of rock's turn back to roots music in 1968.

nashville-skyline.about: A complete turn to country music, made in Nashville, with a soft new crooning voice he put down to having stopped smoking. It was warmly received, gave him his fourth UK number one, and opens with a duet with Johnny Cash on Girl from the North Country. Lay Lady Lay became a top-ten US hit.
nashville-skyline.cover: A smiling Dylan tipping his hat, holding a guitar, photographed by Elliott Landy. The pose echoes a cover by his friend Eric Von Schmidt.
influence: Its success helped open country music to rock artists and audiences, part of the road to country rock.
Dylan appeared on The Johnny Cash Show in June 1969 to promote it.

new-morning.about: Released four months after Self Portrait and far better received, it brought back his familiar voice after two albums of country crooning. It reached number 7 in the US and was his last UK number one until Together Through Life in 2009. If Not for You was also recorded by George Harrison, and Olivia Newton-John had a hit with it.
influence: Olivia Newton-John's version of If Not for You (1971) was her first hit.
George Harrison recorded If Not for You for All Things Must Pass (1970).

self-portrait.about: A double album of cover songs, live recordings and a few new originals, in the country style of Nashville Skyline. Critics and fans were baffled and hostile. Dylan later said part of the point was to confound expectations and shake off the spokesman-of-a-generation label. It has been looked at again since The Bootleg Series Vol. 10 in 2013.
self-portrait.cover: A painting by Dylan himself: a rough self-portrait, which gives the album its name.
influence: It includes performances from his August 1969 Isle of Wight show with the Band, including Like a Rolling Stone.
Its sessions were revisited and widely reappraised on Another Self Portrait (The Bootleg Series Vol. 10, 2013).

bob-dylans-greatest-hits-volume-ii.about: A double compilation that Dylan put together himself, running from Freewheelin' to the 1971 single Watching the River Flow. It also brought out new recordings of songs that had been hits for others, such as I Shall Be Released and You Ain't Goin' Nowhere. It reached the top 20 in the US and UK.
bob-dylans-greatest-hits-volume-ii.cover: Dylan performing at the Concert for Bangladesh in New York in August 1971.
influence: Released as More Bob Dylan Greatest Hits in some countries.

dylan-0.about: Assembled by Columbia from outtakes of the Self Portrait and New Morning sessions, with no input from Dylan, after he had left for Asylum Records. It has six covers and three traditional songs and no Dylan originals, and is widely seen as one of his weakest releases. It was later reissued in Europe as Dylan (A Fool Such as I).
influence: Columbia released it in November 1973, the month his reunion tour with the Band was announced.

pat-garrett-and-billy-the-kid.about: His soundtrack for Sam Peckinpah's western, in which he also played a character called Alias. It is mostly instrumental, recorded in Mexico City and Burbank. Knockin' on Heaven's Door became a top-20 hit on both sides of the Atlantic.
influence: Knockin' on Heaven's Door has been covered by Eric Clapton, Guns N' Roses and many others.
An unfinished outtake sketch from these sessions grew into Old Crow Medicine Show's Wagon Wheel (2004), credited to Dylan as co-writer and later a country number one for Darius Rucker.
Peckinpah's own cut of the film, restored in the 1980s, is now regarded as one of his major works.

before-the-flood.about: His first live album, recorded with the Band on their 1974 US tour, his first major tour since 1966. Released on Asylum, it mixes Dylan's songs with the Band's own sets and reached number 3 in the US.
before-the-flood.cover: An arena audience holding up lit matches and lighters in the dark.
influence: The full tour was later released as The 1974 Live Recordings (2024).

planet-waves.about: Made with the Band in Los Angeles in November 1973, ahead of their reunion tour, and released on Asylum. Boosted by the tour, it became his first US number one album. It includes both a slow and a fast version of Forever Young, written for his children.
planet-waves.cover: A drawing by Dylan. Beside it he wrote the words cast-iron songs & torch ballads, and Moonglow. The handwritten back cover misspells Richard Manuel's name.
influence: Forever Young became one of his most covered songs, recorded by Joan Baez, the Pretenders and many others.
It gave its name to a power in the Japanese manga JoJo's Bizarre Adventure: Stone Ocean.

blood-tracks.about: Recorded in New York in September 1974. In December, shortly before release, he re-recorded five songs in Minneapolis with local musicians, so the album mixes both sessions. The songs are often linked to the breakdown of his marriage, which he has denied. Reviews were mixed at first; it is now ranked among his very best.
blood-tracks.cover: A profile of Dylan facing left, made from a telephoto concert photograph by Paul Till taken in Toronto in January 1974, worked to look like a painting, next to a burgundy title strip.
influence: The original New York sessions came out in full as More Blood, More Tracks (The Bootleg Series Vol. 14, 2018).
Whole-album covers have been recorded by Mary Lee's Corvette (2002) and Ryan Adams (2022).
Tangled Up in Blue became a fixture of his concerts, its words often rewritten from tour to tour.

basement-tapes.about: Songs Dylan and the Band recorded in 1967 in Woodstock, first at his house and then in the basement of a house called Big Pink, while he recovered from his motorcycle accident. Many had circulated on bootlegs for years; this was their first official release, in 1975. Eight of the 24 tracks are by the Band without Dylan, and some were overdubbed for release.
basement-tapes.cover: Dylan and the Band in a basement, actually at a Los Angeles YMCA, among characters suggested by the songs, photographed by Reid Miles.
influence: Made while most of rock was going psychedelic, the 1967 tapes are often cited as a forerunner of Americana.
Songs from them were hits for others before release, such as Manfred Mann's Mighty Quinn and The Byrds' You Ain't Goin' Nowhere.
The complete recordings came out in 2014 as The Bootleg Series Vol. 11.

desire.about: One of his most collaborative records, with the musicians of the Rolling Thunder Revue, Scarlet Rivera's violin and harmonies from Emmylou Harris. Most songs were co-written with Jacques Levy as long story-songs. Hurricane, about the boxer Rubin Carter, was its most famous song and was controversial, as was Joey. It spent five weeks at number one in the US.
influence: Hurricane helped publicise Rubin Carter's case; his conviction was overturned in 1985.
One More Cup of Coffee has been covered by the White Stripes and Robert Plant, among others.

hard-rain.about: A live album from the second, rougher leg of the Rolling Thunder Revue, recorded at two concerts in May 1976 in Fort Worth and Fort Collins. The Fort Collins show was filmed by NBC and shown as a TV special when the album came out. Reviews were mixed.
influence: The NBC special was one of the few times 1970s Dylan was seen on network television.

street-legal.about: Made at Rundown, his own rehearsal space in Santa Monica, with a large band of horns and gospel-style backing singers, produced by Don DeVito. American critics were harsh; British ones were kinder, and Baby, Stop Crying was a UK top-15 hit. A 1999 remix improved the muddy sound, and its reputation has grown since.
influence: Its big-band sound carried into the 1978 world tour, documented on Bob Dylan at Budokan.

bob-dylan-at-budokan.about: Recorded in Tokyo on the 1978 world tour and first released only in Japan, then worldwide in 1979. Big-band rearrangements of his best-known songs, with saxophone, flute and backing singers. Many American critics disliked it; European ones were more positive.
influence: The two complete Budokan shows were released in full as The Complete Budokan 1978 (2023).

slow-train-coming.about: His first album after becoming a born-again Christian, recorded at Muscle Shoals with producers Jerry Wexler and Barry Beckett and Mark Knopfler on guitar. Its evangelism put off many existing fans while drawing in new ones. Gotta Serve Somebody was his first hit in three years and won him the Grammy for best male rock vocal performance.
influence: John Lennon wrote the parody Serve Yourself in response to Gotta Serve Somebody.
It is listed among the greatest albums in Christian music by CCM magazine's 2001 book.

saved.about: The second of his three Christian albums, also made at Muscle Shoals, with full gospel arrangements and a choir of backing singers. It sold poorly in the US, but the songs came alive on the gospel tours of 1979–80.
saved.cover: The original cover was a painting by Tony Wright of the hand of Christ reaching down to the hands of believers. It was later replaced with a painting of Dylan on stage, and has since been restored on some reissues.
influence: The live versions on Trouble No More (The Bootleg Series Vol. 13, 2017) led many listeners to reassess this period.

shot-love.about: The last of the Christian trilogy, mixing faith with other subjects again. Reviews were mixed and US sales were low, though it reached number 6 in the UK. Critics singled out the closing song, Every Grain of Sand, as one of his finest.
influence: Bono of U2 has named it one of his favourite Dylan albums, largely for the singing.
Every Grain of Sand was sung by Emmylou Harris, among others, and has been called one of his greatest late songs.

infidels.about: His return to mostly secular songwriting, co-produced with Mark Knopfler and played by a band including Sly Dunbar and Robbie Shakespeare. Its love songs and pointed commentary on politics and the environment earned his best reviews in years. Blind Willie McTell, left off the album, later became one of his most admired songs when it surfaced in 1991.
influence: Jokerman and Sweetheart Like You were promoted with music videos made for the MTV era.
The outtakes, including Blind Willie McTell, came out in full on Springtime in New York (The Bootleg Series Vol. 16, 2021).

biograph.about: A career box set of 53 tracks from 1962 to 1981, 18 of them previously unreleased, with a long booklet of notes and Dylan's own comments. It was certified platinum.
influence: One of the first career-spanning box sets by a major rock artist, and a model for many that followed.
Its unreleased tracks paved the way for The Bootleg Series from 1991.

empire-burlesque.about: Self-produced, with members of Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers among a long list of session players, and a glossy mid-1980s sound mixed by Arthur Baker. Initial reviews were good; its reputation fell later, largely because of the production. It closes with the acoustic Dark Eyes.
empire-burlesque.cover: Photographed by Ken Regan, designed by Nick Egan.
influence: Tight Connection to My Heart got a video shot in Tokyo, directed by Paul Schrader.

real-live.about: A live album from his 1984 European stadium tour with Santana, recorded mostly at Wembley Stadium on 7 July, with tracks from Newcastle and from Slane Castle in Ireland. Mick Taylor of the Rolling Stones played guitar in the band.
influence: The 1984 tour drew some of his largest European crowds of the decade.

knocked-out-loaded.about: A patchy mix of covers, collaborations and new songs, released during his 1986 tour with Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers. Reviews were poor and sales weak. The exception is Brownsville Girl, an eleven-minute story-song co-written with the playwright Sam Shepard, which many critics count among his best.
knocked-out-loaded.cover: Dylan rejected a design by Rick Griffin and used a reworked 1939 cover of the pulp magazine Spicy Adventure Stories instead. The inner sleeve carries a long, partly surreal list of thanks.
influence: Brownsville Girl grew from an earlier song, New Danville Girl, recorded in 1984.

down-in-the-groove.about: Assembled from sessions spread over five years, mixing covers with four originals, two co-written with the Grateful Dead's lyricist Robert Hunter. Guests include Ronnie Wood, Eric Clapton and members of the Grateful Dead. It was poorly received and sold weakly.
influence: Silvio, one of the Hunter co-writes, became a regular in his concerts for years.

dylan-and-the-dead.about: Seven Dylan songs recorded with the Grateful Dead on their 1987 stadium tour, produced by Jerry Garcia and John Cutler. It sold well at first but was poorly reviewed.
influence: Playing with the Dead and then with Tom Petty helped lead to his Never Ending Tour, which began in June 1988.

oh-mercy.about: Produced by Daniel Lanois in New Orleans, with a dark, atmospheric sound. After a run of weak albums it was hailed as a return to form and was his best chart showing in years. Dylan wrote about making it at length in his memoir Chronicles: Volume One.
oh-mercy.cover: A photograph of a mural of two people dancing that Dylan found on the wall of a Chinese restaurant in Hell's Kitchen, Manhattan. The muralist, who signed himself Trotsky, was traced and gave permission.
influence: Lanois went on to produce Time Out of Mind (1997).
Outtakes such as Series of Dreams and Dignity later became fan favourites.

under-red-sky.about: Produced by Don and David Was with Dylan (credited as Jack Frost), with guests including George Harrison, Elton John, Slash, David Crosby and Stevie Ray Vaughan. Several songs borrow the shape of nursery rhymes. It was seen as a disappointment after Oh Mercy, and Wiggle Wiggle often lands on lists of his worst songs.
influence: After it, he went back to traditional songs, alone with a guitar, on Good as I Been to You (1992).

the-bootleg-series-vol-1-3-rare-and-unre.about: The first of the Bootleg Series: 58 outtakes, demos and live recordings from 1961 to 1989. It made official many recordings fans had only known from bootlegs, including Blind Willie McTell and Series of Dreams.
influence: It started the archive series that has since become the main way his unreleased work comes out.
It established Blind Willie McTell as one of his most admired songs.

good-i-been-you.about: Traditional folk songs and covers, recorded alone at his home studio in Malibu with guitar and harmonica: his first fully solo acoustic album since 1964. Its modest scale won surprisingly warm reviews, with praise for his phrasing.
influence: It began a return to the roots repertoire that fed his later songwriting.

the-30th-anniversary-concert-celebration.about: A Madison Square Garden concert on 16 October 1992 marking 30 years since his first album, with dozens of artists singing his songs, backed by Booker T. & the M.G.'s, Jim Keltner and G. E. Smith as musical director. Dylan himself closes the night.
influence: Performers included Stevie Wonder, Neil Young, Eric Clapton, George Harrison, Lou Reed, Johnny Cash, June Carter Cash, Tom Petty and Pearl Jam's Eddie Vedder.
Sinéad O'Connor was loudly booed and sang Bob Marley's War in place of her planned Dylan song, a widely reported moment of the night.

world-gone-wrong.about: A second album of traditional songs, alone with guitar and harmonica, darker in mood than Good as I Been to You. Dylan wrote his own notes on the songs' sources. It won the Grammy for best traditional folk album.
world-gone-wrong.cover: Dylan in a top hat at a table in a café in Camden Town, London, photographed by Ana Maria Velez, with a painting behind him.
influence: Critics in the Village Voice poll and at AllMusic ranked it among his strongest later records.

greatest-hits-volume-3.about: A single-disc compilation covering the mid-1970s to the early 1990s, with one previously unreleased song, Dignity, an Oh Mercy outtake.

mtv-unplugged.about: Recorded for MTV's Unplugged series at Sony Music Studios in New York over two nights in November 1994, with his touring band playing acoustic. It gave him his best sales in years: number 23 in the US and number 10 in the UK.

time-out-of-mind.about: His first album of new songs in seven years, recorded in Miami with Daniel Lanois producing: dark, swampy and full of thoughts of age and loss. It was widely hailed as a comeback and won three Grammys, including Album of the Year. Shortly after it was finished he became seriously ill with a fungal infection of the heart lining, which added to the album's aura when it came out.
influence: Make You Feel My Love became a standard, recorded by Billy Joel, Garth Brooks and, most famously, Adele (2008).
The sessions were revisited on Fragments (The Bootleg Series Vol. 17, 2023), including a remix of the album without Lanois's production effects.

bootleg-series-vol-4-bob-dylan-live-1966.about: The famous 17 May 1966 concert at the Free Trade Hall in Manchester, long mislabelled on bootlegs as the Royal Albert Hall show. Half acoustic and solo, half electric with the Hawks, it ends with a shout of Judas from the audience and a furious Like a Rolling Stone. Bootlegged for decades, it was finally released in 1998.
influence: One of the most famous bootlegs in rock; Jimmy Page reportedly bought copies whenever he saw one.
Cat Power re-created the whole concert on stage and on record in 2023.
It is included in 1001 Albums You Must Hear Before You Die.

essential-bob-dylan.about: A two-disc career overview in Sony's Essential series, running from Blowin' in the Wind to Things Have Changed, his Oscar-winning song for the film Wonder Boys. Track lists vary by country and reissue.
influence: It was the first title in Sony Music's long-running Essential series.

love-and-theft.about: Recorded with his touring band and Augie Meyers on keyboards, a mix of blues, swing, rockabilly and Tin Pan Alley balladry, self-produced as Jack Frost. It was released on 11 September 2001 and topped critics' polls that year. It won the Grammy for best contemporary folk album.
love-and-theft.cover: A black-and-white studio portrait with a new pencil moustache, by Kevin Mazur.
influence: The title, in quotation marks, nods to Eric Lott's book about blackface minstrelsy, Love & Theft.
Lines echoing a Japanese gangster memoir, Confessions of a Yakuza, were noticed after release and started a long debate about his borrowing.
It topped the Village Voice Pazz & Jop critics' poll, the third Dylan album to do so.

bootleg-series-vol-5-bob-dylan-live-1975.about: Highlights from the first leg of the Rolling Thunder Revue in late 1975, the travelling show that preceded Desire. Until then, the only official record of the tour was the rougher Hard Rain. Fans welcomed it, though it does not follow a full show.
influence: The complete 1975 recordings followed in 2019, alongside Martin Scorsese's film Rolling Thunder Revue.

bootleg-series-vol-6-bob-dylan-live-1964.about: The complete Halloween 1964 concert at Philharmonic Hall in New York, solo acoustic, relaxed and joking, with Joan Baez joining him for several songs. It caught him between protest singer and the electric years.
influence: It includes early live versions of Mr. Tambourine Man and It's Alright, Ma (I'm Only Bleeding), before either was released.

the-best-of-bob-dylan.about: A single-disc best-of from 2005, packaged in a mock vinyl sleeve, with notes by Bill Flanagan on each track.

bootleg-series-vol-7-no-direction-home.about: The companion to Martin Scorsese's 2005 documentary No Direction Home, compiled with Scorsese's input. It covers 1959 to the 1966 world tour, mostly with previously unreleased takes and live recordings.
influence: Scorsese's film, built around Dylan's own interviews, became a standard account of his early years.
It includes a 1959 home recording from Minnesota, at the time the earliest Dylan recording released.

modern-times.about: Self-produced as Jack Frost with his touring band, continuing the blues, rockabilly and pre-rock ballads of the previous two albums. At 65 it made him the oldest living artist to debut at number one on the US chart, his first chart-topper there since Desire. Its uncredited borrowings from older songs and from the poets Henry Timrod and Ovid sparked debate.
modern-times.cover: Ted Croner's 1947 photograph Taxi, New York at Night.
influence: Rolling Stone named it album of the year for 2006.
It won two Grammys, including best contemporary folk/Americana album.

dylan.about: A career compilation from 2007, released as a single disc and as a three-disc deluxe set of 51 songs in replica-vinyl packaging with postcards and a booklet.
influence: Its launch included an online tool that let fans put their own words into the Subterranean Homesick Blues cue-card film.

bootleg-series-vol-8-tell-tale-signs.about: Outtakes, alternate versions, soundtrack songs and live tracks from 1989 to 2006, the Oh Mercy era to Modern Times. Several outtakes, including alternate takes of Mississippi and Most of the Time, were judged by many to rival the released versions.
influence: It changed how his late period was heard, showing how far songs changed between takes and albums.

christmas-heart.about: Hymns, carols and popular Christmas songs, produced by Dylan himself. All his royalties go, in perpetuity, to Feeding America, Crisis in the UK and the World Food Programme. Raised Jewish in Minnesota, he said he had never felt left out of Christmas.
christmas-heart.cover: An antique print of a sleigh ride through snow; the inner sleeve shows four musicians in Santa suits, photographed by Leonard Freed.
influence: The polka-style video for Must Be Santa, a party scene with Dylan in a wig, became a seasonal favourite.

together-through-life.about: Unexpected when it arrived, with most songs co-written with the Grateful Dead's lyricist Robert Hunter and accordion from David Hidalgo of Los Lobos giving it a border-town feel. It started as a song for Olivier Dahan's film My Own Love Song. It went to number one in the US and UK.
together-through-life.cover: Bruce Davidson's 1959 photograph of a young couple kissing in the back seat of a car.
influence: It was his first UK number one album since New Morning in 1970.

best-original-mono-recordings.about: A single-disc selection from The Original Mono Recordings box, gathering highlights of his first eight albums as they were first mixed in mono.

bootleg-series-vol-9-witmark-demos-1962-.about: 47 demos he recorded for his first music publishers, Leeds Music and M. Witmark & Sons, between 1962 and 1964, alone with guitar, harmonica and sometimes piano. They were made so other artists could learn the songs, and 15 were never recorded any other way.
influence: Peter, Paul and Mary and many others first heard his songs through demos like these.

original-mono-recordings.about: His first eight studio albums as they were originally mixed in mono, on nine CDs and on vinyl, with a booklet and essay by Greil Marcus. For most of the 1960s, mono was the mix that Dylan and the producers concentrated on.

bob-dylan-in-concert-brandeis-university.about: A short set at the Brandeis Folk Festival in Waltham, Massachusetts, on 10 May 1963, found on tape in the archive of the critic Ralph Gleason, a co-founder of Rolling Stone, after his death. It is the last live recording before he became a star; Freewheelin' came out weeks later.
influence: First offered as a bonus disc in 2010, it was released on its own in 2011.

tempest.about: Recorded at Jackson Browne's studio in Santa Monica with his touring band, every song his own except Duquesne Whistle, co-written with Robert Hunter. Critics praised its dark, long story-songs, including a fourteen-minute ballad about the Titanic and a tribute to John Lennon. It was his last album of new songs until 2020.
tempest.cover: A deep red photograph of the statue representing the river Moldau at the Pallas-Athene Fountain in front of the Austrian Parliament in Vienna.
influence: Roll On John is a tribute to John Lennon; Tempest itself retells the sinking of the Titanic over fourteen minutes.

bootleg-series-vol-10-another-self-portr.about: Outtakes, demos and alternate takes from the Self Portrait and New Morning sessions, plus Isle of Wight live tracks, mostly stripped of their original overdubs. It turned one of his most derided periods into one of the most praised releases of the series.
influence: The notes are by Greil Marcus, who wrote the famously scathing Rolling Stone review of Self Portrait in 1970.
It led many to reassess Self Portrait itself.

30th-anniversary-concert-celebration-del.about: An expanded 2014 reissue of the 1992 Madison Square Garden tribute concert, adding performances left off the original release, with the full concert on video.

bootleg-series-vol-11-basement-tapes-com.about: All 138 surviving recordings Dylan and the musicians who became the Band made in Woodstock in 1967, 117 of them previously unreleased, restored from the original tapes. For decades these were the holy grail of Dylan collectors.
influence: Songs from these sessions filled Great White Wonder (1969), often called the first rock bootleg album.
The rediscovery of unfinished lyrics from 1967 led to Lost on the River (2014), with Elvis Costello, Marcus Mumford, Jim James and others writing music for them.

bootleg-series-vol-11-basement-tapes-raw.about: The two-disc highlights edition of The Basement Tapes Complete: the 1967 Woodstock home recordings with the musicians who became the Band, without the overdubs added for the 1975 album.

shadows-in-the-night-2.about: Ten pop standards that Frank Sinatra had recorded, arranged for his small touring band with pedal steel and a few horns, recorded live in the studio. Critics praised the arrangements and the care of his singing. In the UK it entered at number one, making him the oldest male solo artist to top the album chart there.
shadows-in-the-night-2.cover: Dylan in shadow behind vertical bars, a design echoing Freddie Hubbard's 1962 Blue Note album Hub-Tones.
influence: Dylan sent 50000 copies free to AARP members, America's organisation for older people, and gave a long interview to its magazine.

the-bootleg-series-vol-12-the-best-of-th.about: Highlights from the 1965–66 studio sessions for Bringing It All Back Home, Highway 61 Revisited and Blonde on Blonde: rehearsals, false starts and alternate takes that show the songs taking shape.

the-bootleg-series-vol-12-the-cutting-ed.about: The six-disc edition of The Cutting Edge, with every take from the 1965–66 sessions in the main set's selection of songs, and an 18-disc collector's edition with everything from the sessions.
influence: It documents every take of Like a Rolling Stone, including the shift from waltz time to the released rock arrangement.

fallen-angels.about: A second album of American standards, all but one once sung by Sinatra, by writers such as Johnny Mercer and Harold Arlen. Reviews praised his singing and the band's arrangements.
fallen-angels.cover: A cropped vintage photograph, from 1928, of a man holding a hand of cards.
influence: Mojo placed it among the best albums of 2016.

triplicate.about: Thirty standards across three discs, each a themed ten-song set, recorded live in the studio with his touring band and no overdubs. Reviews were strongly positive. It was the last of his three albums of standards.
triplicate.cover: Only the title, in white blackletter on deep purple: the plainest cover in his catalogue.
influence: It carries liner notes by the novelist Tom Piazza, the first in a Dylan studio album since 1993.

trouble-no-more-the-bootleg-series-vol-1.about: Live and studio recordings from his gospel years, 1979 to 1981, when his concerts were made up of new religious songs. The live versions, with a strong band and gospel singers, convinced many that this music was far better than its reputation.
influence: The deluxe set includes a film combining concert footage with new sermons written by Luc Sante and performed by Michael Shannon.

live-1962-1966-rare-performances-from-th.about: A two-disc set of live recordings from 1962 to 1966, from folk clubs and concert halls through the 1966 tour, drawn from limited copyright-protection releases. It first came out in Japan in 2018.

more-blood-more-tracks-the-bootleg-serie.about: The single-disc edition of the Blood on the Tracks sessions: the New York recordings of September 1974 as they sounded before Dylan re-cut five songs in Minneapolis. Mostly just voice, guitar and bass, closer and quieter than the album.
influence: Before this, only a handful of the New York outtakes had been released, scattered across Biograph and The Bootleg Series Vol. 1–3.

more-blood-more-tracks-the-bootleg-serie.about: Every surviving take from the September 1974 New York sessions for Blood on the Tracks, in session order across six discs, plus the December Minneapolis masters. You can hear the songs, and their words, change from take to take.

bob-dylan-the-rolling-thunder-revue-the-.about: Five complete Rolling Thunder Revue concerts from autumn 1975 plus rehearsals and rarities, on 14 discs. The band, a loose collective, was nicknamed Guam. It came out a week before Martin Scorsese's Netflix film Rolling Thunder Revue: A Bob Dylan Story.
influence: Scorsese's film mixed real concert footage with invented characters and staged interviews, a playful nod to the tour's masks and face paint.

the-bootleg-series-vol-15-travelin-thru-.about: Outtakes from John Wesley Harding and Nashville Skyline, and the full February 1969 sessions with Johnny Cash in Nashville, plus his appearance on The Johnny Cash Show and recordings with Earl Scruggs.
influence: The Dylan–Cash sessions had long circulated on bootleg; this was their first full release.

rough-and-rowdy-ways.about: His first album of new songs since Tempest, recorded at Sound City in Los Angeles in early 2020 with his touring band plus Blake Mills and Fiona Apple. It closes with Murder Most Foul, a nearly seventeen-minute song about the assassination of John F. Kennedy, released first, in March 2020, which became his first song to top a Billboard chart. It drew the highest reviews of his late career.
rough-and-rowdy-ways.cover: A tinted 1964 photograph by Ian Berry of a couple dancing by a jukebox in a club on Cable Street in Whitechapel, London. The title echoes a 1929 song by Jimmie Rodgers.
influence: It topped many 2020 best-of lists, including Mojo and Uncut.
At 79 it made him the first artist with a top-40 US album in each decade since the 1960s.

springtime-in-new-york-the-bootleg-serie.about: Rehearsals, outtakes and live tracks from 1980 to 1985: the Shot of Love, Infidels and Empire Burlesque sessions, with stripped-back versions that many prefer to the released ones. It reached number 6 in the UK.
influence: It includes alternate Infidels-era takes of songs such as Jokerman and Too Late, the early form of Foot of Pride.

shadow-kingdom.about: The soundtrack to Shadow Kingdom, a black-and-white film directed by Alma Har'el and shot on a Santa Monica soundstage in 2021 while touring was stopped by the pandemic. Dylan and masked musicians rework thirteen songs from the first half of his career in a smoky club setting. First streamed online in 2021, it came out as an album in 2023.
influence: Viewers who expected a live concert got a stylised art film, which critics praised for its reworked arrangements.

the-bootleg-series-vol-17-fragments-time.about: The Time Out of Mind sessions revisited: a new remix of the album that strips back Daniel Lanois's layers of effects, plus outtakes, alternate versions and live performances from 1997 to 2001.
influence: The remix let listeners compare the album with and without its famous murky production.

the-complete-budokan-1978.about: Both full concerts from the Nippon Budokan in Tokyo, 28 February and 1 March 1978, restored and remixed, from which the original Bob Dylan at Budokan was drawn. The previously unreleased tracks also appeared on vinyl as Another Budokan.

the-1974-live-recordings.about: A 27-CD box of every known soundboard recording from Dylan and the Band's 1974 tour of the US and Canada, most previously unreleased, including the full shows used for Before the Flood. The Band's own songs from the shows are left out.
influence: It came with a two-disc sampler and the first official release of much of the tour.

the-bootleg-series-vol-18-bob-dylans-boo.about: His earliest recordings, from a 1956 recording made with school friends in St. Paul, Minnesota, through his Greenwich Village years to 1963. The deluxe edition includes the whole of his October 1963 concert at Carnegie Hall.
influence: It covers the period shown in the 2024 film A Complete Unknown, which takes up his story in 1961.

the-rolling-thunder-revue-the-1976-live-.about: Released on 6 November 2026: 39 discs and 381 tracks from the second leg of the Rolling Thunder Revue in April and May 1976, 371 of them previously unreleased. The Fort Worth show of 16 May 1976 also came out on its own as a triple LP.
influence: Together with the 1975 box, it completes the official record of the Rolling Thunder tours; before, the 1976 leg was known mainly from Hard Rain.
